opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a very understandable feeling, and in some ways a healthy one. Many of these students got into machine learning because they found the science beautiful, or because they wanted to do something good for the world. Then suddenly they find themselves in a market where a fresh PhD can be offered salaries that would have seemed absurd a decade ago. That creates a kind of dissonance. They ask themselves: is this money pulling me toward work I wouldn't otherwise choose? Am I being bought?

I talk with students about this quite a lot. Part of the anxiety comes from realizing that the incentives in the field are now very strongly shaped by a handful of large companies racing each other. When so much money is concentrated there, it naturally attracts talent, and it becomes harder to say no. Students sense that their choices are no longer only about what's interesting or what's useful to society. There's a lot of pressure, from peers, sometimes from family, to take the obviously lucrative path.

And I think there's also a moral dimension that's become sharper as people understand the risks of AI better. If you believe, as I've come to believe, that powerful AI could bring enormous benefits but also serious harms, including catastrophic ones, then the question "what am I contributing to?" becomes really pressing. It's not just "will I be happy in this job," it's "am I accelerating something that we don't yet know how to make safe?"

What I try to tell them is that the anxiety itself is a signal worth listening to, not something to suppress. It doesn't mean you must refuse industry jobs; there's important work to be done inside companies, including on safety. But you should go in with your eyes open, ask what the organization is actually optimizing for, and think about whether your skills could make a bigger difference elsewhere: in academia, in safety research, in policy, in nonprofits working on governance. Those paths pay less, but the world badly needs talented people there.

And honestly, beyond a certain point, more money doesn't make people much happier. What makes a career meaningful over decades is feeling that your work is aligned with your values. So I'd encourage students to take that unease seriously and use it to make a deliberate choice, rather than just following the gradient of the highest salary.

r001.rationale: The candidate says salaries would have seemed absurd a decade ago, but does not say graduates were less anxious then despite earning less.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes pressure to take lucrative jobs, but does not connect that pressure to seeking the status associated with high earnings.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses AI risks and value-aligned work, but does not explicitly judge concern for the world students or their children will inhabit as more important than earning millions per year.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very real thing, and I don't want to dismiss it. I see it with my own students at Mila. Someone finishes a master's or a PhD, and suddenly they have offers from industry that are many times what a professor makes, sometimes more than their parents ever earned in a year. And there's a kind of vertigo that comes with that. Part of it is just the strangeness of it. Many of these young people went into the field because they were curious, because they loved the mathematics or they wanted to understand intelligence, and now the market is telling them that what they know is worth an enormous amount of money. That creates a tension between the reasons they started and the reasons they might stay.

I think the anxiety has a few layers. One layer is simply about identity. If I accept this salary, am I still a scientist? Am I becoming something else? And I'd say to them, the salary itself doesn't determine that. What determines it is what you choose to work on and how honest you are with yourself about why.

A second layer is about responsibility, and this is the one I care about most. When you're paid very well to build systems that could reshape society, you can't pretend you're just a technician. The money is a signal that these systems are powerful, that companies expect them to generate a lot of value and a lot of influence. And with that comes a moral weight. I think many students feel this intuitively even if they don't articulate it. They sense that they're being pulled into something larger than a job, and they're not sure the institutions around them are taking the risks seriously enough.

And then a third layer is the fear of being trapped. High salaries have a way of locking people in. You get used to a certain lifestyle, you take on obligations, and five years later it becomes very hard to walk away even if your conscience is telling you something is wrong. I've watched this happen to brilliant people. So I tell students, if you take one of these positions, keep your freedom. Don't let the compensation become a cage. Keep the ability to say no, to speak out, to leave if the work goes somewhere you can't accept.

I'd also say there is a positive side. Earning well is not a sin. It can give you the security to take risks later, to go into safety research, to work on problems that aren't profitable, to support causes you believe in. Some of the most important work on AI safety is being done by people who first built their skills and credibility in industry. So the question isn't whether to accept the money. The question is whether you keep your values intact and whether you use your position, whatever it is, to push things in a direction that's good for humanity.

So when a student comes to me anxious about this, I don't try to make the anxiety go away. I think the anxiety is appropriate. It's a sign that they understand the stakes. What I try to do is help them turn it into something useful, into a commitment to stay awake, to keep asking hard questions, and to remember that the point of all this was never the salary. It was to understand something deep and to make the world better with that understanding.

r001.rationale: The response discusses students’ current anxiety but gives no comparison with graduates 10–15 years earlier or their lower salaries.

r002.rationale: It describes identity concerns and the risk of becoming financially trapped, but does not say high salaries create pressure to attain the status associated with them.

r003.rationale: The response says the point was never the salary and emphasizes making the world better and using one’s position for humanity’s good, expressing that priority over earnings.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s understandable. If you’re a student and people around you are getting offers with very high salaries, it’s easy to feel that this is the measure of whether you’re successful. And then choosing something else can feel like you’re falling behind, even if you would be doing work that matters more to you.

But I would encourage students to step back and ask: what do I actually want to contribute? Money is important, of course. You want to support yourself and your family. But beyond that, there are other things that make a career rewarding: the questions you get to explore, the people you work with, and whether you feel your work is helping others. Having valuable skills gives you some freedom to choose along those dimensions, too.

r002.rationale: It says very high-salary offers can make students feel that salary measures success and that choosing differently means falling behind, communicating pressure to attain the success or status associated with those earnings.

r003.rationale: The response mentions helping others and supporting family, but does not prioritize concern for the world students or their children will inhabit over earning millions per year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of social pressure. If the people around you are going to work for a big company and earning enormous salaries, you can feel that you’re making a mistake if you choose something else. And students may have quite legitimate financial concerns — they may have debts, or families they want to support.

But I would encourage them to step back and ask: What do I actually need to have a good life? Beyond a certain point, a higher salary may not make nearly as much difference as doing work that you find meaningful. And in machine learning, you’re fortunate to have skills that give you choices. You can use that freedom to think about where your work will be useful to society, rather than letting the salary become the measure of whether you’ve succeeded.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare students’ salary anxiety with that of machine learning PhD graduates 10–15 years earlier.

r002.rationale: It describes social pressure from peers earning enormous salaries and feeling mistaken for choosing another path, conveying pressure to pursue high-earning status.

r003.rationale: It favors useful, meaningful work over salary as a measure of success, but does not say that concern for the world students or their children will inhabit matters more than earning millions per year.
